title: Spin-orbit coupling by design in quantum state engineering of atomically defined quantum dots
authors: Hermann Osterhage, Julian H. Strik, Ivan Ado, Anna M. H. Krieg, Daniel Wegner, Mikhail Titov, Alexander A. Khajetoorians
abstract: Tuning spin-orbit coupling is essential in controlling both spin and charge in confined semiconductor nanostructures, yet it is rarely a truly controllable parameter. Here, we show control over the spin-orbit Hamiltonian in quantum dots and the resulting quantum states by tailoring the confinement potential with atomic-scale precision. Using scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy, we pattern individual Cs ions into designer quantum dot structures on the surface of indium antimonide, in which electrons from a two-dimensional electron gas are confined with chosen in-plane electric-field gradients. We then quantify the atomic level structure, both spatially resolving the orbital character of the electronic states and their magnetic-field evolution. We demonstrate that the level structure, including the induced zero-field splitting, can be tailored by the designed geometry of the local electric fields. These effects can be described using a Hamiltonian that allows consistent treatment of the confinement-induced spin-orbit coupling beyond the conventional Bychkov-Rashba description. This Hamiltonian is derived from a multiband k.p model and takes the energy dependence of the relevant physical parameters into account. Such precise control of spin-orbit coupling in semiconductor quantum dots is relevant to quantum and spintronic technologies.
summary: This research demonstrates the ability to engineer and control spin-orbit coupling in semiconductor quantum dots by precisely tailoring their confining electric potentials at the atomic scale. By combining STM/STS measurements with advanced k.p theory, the authors successfully model and verify that SOC dictates measurable energy splittings and magnetic responses, paving the way for next-generation spintronic devices.
main_problem: The central problem is achieving precise, controllable tuning of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) within atomically defined semiconductor quantum dots (QDs). This control moves beyond simple approximations by tailoring the local electrostatic confinement potential.
main_result: The study demonstrates that SOC-induced energy splittings and magnetic responses in QDs can be accurately predicted and controlled by designing the geometry of the confining electric fields, matching experimental observations across isotropic and anisotropic potentials.
method: The research combines advanced Scanning Tunneling Microscopy/Spectroscopy (STM/STS) measurements with theoretical modeling based on an effective Hamiltonian derived from a multiband k.p model.
model_or_system: The physical system is electron confinement in InSb surface quantum dots, engineered by patterning individual Cs ions to create designer electrostatic potentials. The theory uses an effective Hamiltonian incorporating kinetic energy, parabolic/triangular confinement potentials, Zeeman terms, and SOC terms beyond the standard Rashba description.
key_observables: Zero-field splitting (ZFS) of electronic states, magnetic field dependence of energy levels ($	ext{d}I/	ext{dV}$ spectra), and spatial decay profiles of the ground state wavefunction.
important_parameters: Confinement strengths ($\kappa_x, \kappa_y$), SOC coupling constants ($\lambda_{	ext{SOC}}$), effective electron mass ($m^*$), and magnetic field strength ($B$).
main_assumptions: The model relies on approximating the confinement potential as a sum of triangular and parabolic terms, and treating SOC perturbatively to an effective Hamiltonian.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate STM images and $	ext{d}I/	ext{dV}$ maps for QDs with varying geometries (circular vs. anisotropic), showing characteristic energy splittings and wavefunction spatial decay patterns under applied magnetic fields.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the experimental platform (Cs patterning on InSb) and measurement techniques (STM/STS). It then develops a generalized theoretical Hamiltonian incorporating SOC, solving it for both isotropic and anisotropic confinement regimes to predict measurable energy splittings and spatial features.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete example of how fundamental solid-state physics concepts (SOC) can be experimentally manipulated using nanoscale electrostatic engineering, offering pathways toward realizing controllable spin qubits in semiconductor platforms relevant to quantum information science.
